blocks.passage:
Negotiating an international contract is less about winning words and more about making sure both sides understand the same thing. A poorly drafted contract leaves both parties convinced they agreed to something — only to discover, months later, that 'something' meant two different things.

The most important clauses are usually the quiet ones: governing law (whose court decides?), dispute resolution (arbitration or court?), force majeure (what counts as a real emergency?), and termination (who can stop the deal, and when?). These clauses rarely matter until they matter absolutely.

Good negotiators read every clause twice: once to understand what it says, once to imagine what could go wrong. The second reading is where the real negotiation happens.

items.q: What is negotiating an international contract mostly about?
options: Making sure both sides understand the same thing
items.why: "less about winning words and more about making sure both sides understand the same thing."

items.q: What does a poorly drafted contract lead to?
options: Both parties discovering 'something' meant two different things
items.why: "'something' meant two different things."

items.q: Which is described as one of the 'quiet' but most important clauses?
items.why: "governing law (whose court decides?)" é uma das cláusulas quietas mais importantes.

items.q: What does the force majeure clause define?
options: What counts as a real emergency
items.why: "force majeure (what counts as a real emergency?)."

items.q: What is the 'second reading' of each clause for?
options: To imagine what could go wrong
items.why: "once to imagine what could go wrong. The second reading is where the real negotiation happens."

audio.text:
I'm reviewing the draft contract with our Asian counterparty, and I'm reading it twice — once for what it says, once for what could go wrong. The two clauses I care most about are governing law and dispute resolution.

Right now the draft says the governing law is their home country, and any dispute goes to their local court. Think about what that means if we ever disagree: we'd be fighting a case in a foreign legal system, in another language, on their home ground. That's a real disadvantage, and it's quiet — it doesn't matter at all until the day it matters absolutely.

So I'm not signing this as it stands. My counter-proposal is neutral ground: governing law of a third country that both sides respect, and disputes settled by international arbitration rather than either side's local court. Neutral for them, neutral for us.

This isn't me being difficult. If the deal goes well, none of this ever comes up. But contracts exist for the day it doesn't go well — and on that day, you want to have read the quiet clauses twice.

items.q: How is Charlotte reading the draft contract?
options: Twice — once for what it says, once for what could go wrong
items.why: "I'm reading it twice — once for what it says, once for what could go wrong."

items.q: What does the current draft say about governing law and disputes?
options: Their home country's law, disputes in their local court
items.why: "the governing law is their home country, and any dispute goes to their local court."

items.q: Why is that a disadvantage for Charlotte's side?
options: They'd fight a case in a foreign system, in another language, on the other side's home ground
items.why: "we'd be fighting a case in a foreign legal system, in another language, on their home ground."

items.q: What is Charlotte's counter-proposal?
options: Neutral governing law and international arbitration
items.why: "governing law of a third country that both sides respect, and disputes settled by international arbitration."

items.q: Why does Charlotte say the quiet clauses matter?
options: Contracts exist for the day the deal doesn't go well
items.why: "contracts exist for the day it doesn't go well."

items.q: The **governing law** of a contract is…
options: the legal system that applies to it
items.why: Governing law = lei aplicável.

items.q: **Arbitration** is…
options: settling a dispute through a neutral arbitrator instead of a court
items.why: Arbitration = arbitragem.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "The **___** clause says who can end the deal and when."
items.why: Termination = rescisão.

items.q: **Force majeure** covers…
options: extraordinary events beyond a party's control
items.why: Force majeure = força maior.

items.q: Choose the correct term: "A vague clause creates **___** about what was agreed."
items.why: Ambiguity = ambiguidade.

items.q: "I'm not signing this **as it stands**." As it stands means…
items.why: As it stands = como está atualmente.

items.q: "That clause never **comes up** if the deal goes well." To come up means to…
items.why: Come up = surgir, tornar-se relevante.

items.q: "Let's settle disputes on **neutral ground**." Neutral ground means…
items.why: Neutral ground = terreno neutro.

items.q: "This isn't me **being difficult**." To be difficult means to…
items.why: Being difficult = criando dificuldade.

items.q: "It doesn't matter **until it matters absolutely**." This phrase stresses that a clause is…
options: unimportant until a crisis, then critical
items.why: Ideia: quieto até o dia em que se torna decisivo.
